newsitem.title: USA: Israeli leader begins four-day visit to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Israeli leader begins four-day visit to U.S..

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began a four-day U.S. visit on Wednesday during which he and President Bill Clinton hoped to draw up a blueprint for future Middle East peace moves.

Calling the process "a work in progress," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton was anxious to build on the momemtum of the recent Israeli-Palestinian agreement on redeployment of troops in Hebron.
"That was, in a sense, a hurdle for the parties themselves to cross so that they could then move on to other issues that are embedded in the process," McCurry told reporters.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told a Congressional committee on Wednesday that the Hebron accord provided "a very important benchmark" and could be the stepping stone to wider agreement.

Netanyahu, who arrived in Washington on Wednesday night, reached his first agreement with the Palestinians last month when he closed a deal handing over most of the volatile West Bank town to Palestine Liberation Organisation rule.
Israeli officials said Netanyahu, too, was looking to his meeting with Clinton "to see where the strategy for the Middle East peace process turns."

The two leaders were expected to exchange views on how to advance the process as well as what might be done to revive talks between Israel and Syria, although McCurry said he did not expect major developments on that front.

Negotiations with Syria, regarded as the linchpin in an overall Middle East peace, have stalled over the fate of the strategic Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. Damascus has demanded the area be returned.
Netanyahu said on Wednesday Syria had to decide itself if it wanted to resume peace talks, adding that he did not expect Washington to bring Damascus to the negotiating table.

"Syria has to make a decision. Does it want peace. If it wants peace it can come to the peace table very quickly. If it doesn't want peace, it will find ways to obstruct the resumption of the talks," he told reporters at a stopover in Amsterdam en route to Washington.

Netanyahu, in expressing concern about a possible Clinton administration deal to sell F-16 fighter aircraft to key U.S. ally Saudi Arabia, also set the stage for at least one touchy issue during his talks with the president, Albright and Defence Secretary William Cohen.
"We view this with severity," declared Netanyahu. "Arming Saudi Arabia with 100 advanced planes and advanced weaponry is a violation of the strategic balance in the Middle East."
But the White House appeared to dismiss the issue as a potential sore point.

"I'm not sure what the potentiality of that sale is at this point ... and if the prime minister raises it, I'm sure the president will respond in a way that makes clear and reaffirms our longstanding commitment to the security of Israel," McCurry said.
Albright also pledged U.S. commitment to the safety and security of Israel.
"America will continue to stand with the peacemakers and against the bomb-throwers in this strategic region," she told the congressional panel.

Netanyahu's visit is the first by several Middle East leaders over the next few weeks. He will be followed by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and King Hussein of Jordan.
